title: Improving Diagnosis in Cognitive Disorders
author: Laura Mcwhirter
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.z97f99n
materials: A significant proportion – between 12% and 70%, but generally around 30% – of symptomatic patients attending memory clinics do not have dementia (Almeida, Hill, Howard, & O’Brien, 1993; Berrios & Hodges, 2000; Pennington, Hayre, Newson, & Coulthard, 2015; Schmidtke, Pohlmann, & Metternich, 2008). Although a range of differential diagnoses may be considered for these patients who have cognitive symptoms without evidence of neurodegenerative disease (neurological illness, medical illness, impairment due to medication, and surgery), review of the literature suggests a significant proportion have cognitive symptoms with a functional (psychogenic) basis. Furthermore, studies from UK memory clinics seem to confirm our clinical experience that the proportion of patients presenting with non-organic memory complaints is increasing. In Liverpool the proportion increased from 50.8% between 2002-4 to 67.1% in 2008-2009 and 70.2% between 2009-10 (Hussey, Foy, & Meehan, 2009; Menon & Larner, 2011). In Sheffield, the proportion of patients attending who did not fulfil criteria for any organic memory problem increased from 35% of all attendees in 2004 and 2006 to 55% in 2012 (Blackburn et al., 2014; Le Couteur et al., 2013).

steps.title: Identify eligible participants
steps.instruction: Screen all patients presenting to the City of Edinburgh Memory Assessment and Treatment Service, the Neurology Department of the Western General Hospital, or the Neuropsychiatry Department of the Western General Hospital for eligibility.

substeps.instruction: Inclusion: predominantly cognitive symptoms, age >18 years, able to give informed consent.

Exclusion: (a) severe cognitive impairment with a probable Alzheimer’s type dementia or other dementia syndrome (per McKhann criteria), (b) does not speak English, (c) severe psychiatric disorder (active suicide risk, severe personality disorder, or psychosis), (d) evidence or strong clinical suspicion of factitious disorder.

steps.title: Recruit participants from three sources
steps.instruction: Approach eligible patients in neurology outpatient clinics, neuropsychiatry clinics, and the Memory Assessment and Treatment Service (MATS) for study participation.

substeps.instruction: The consultant who performed the clinical assessment (neurologist or psychiatrist) determines suitability.
If eligible, the consultant provides the Participant Information Sheet (PIS) and explains the study at the end of the appointment.
The patient is offered the option to be contacted by a researcher; they may take the PIS away and contact the researcher later using the provided details.

steps.title: Researcher contact and detailed explanation
steps.instruction: Contact patients who have consented to be approached and give a full verbal explanation of the study.

substeps.instruction: Dr Laura McWhirter calls the patient after at least 24 hours (or after at least 5 days for participants identified via the e‑Register) by the participant’s preferred method (telephone, post, or email).
Explain study aims, procedures, time commitment, and answer any questions.

steps.title: Obtain verbal consent
steps.instruction: Secure verbal consent over the telephone before any study‑specific procedures are scheduled.

substeps.instruction: Confirm the participant has read the PIS and understands the study.
Record that the participant verbally agrees to take part and to arrange a research appointment.

steps.title: Schedule research assessment
steps.instruction: Arrange a single research assessment to occur within eight weeks of the participant’s standard clinical assessment.

substeps.instruction: Location may be the Centre for Dementia Prevention (clinical research facility), the Outpatient Department of Clinical Neurosciences, or a home visit by researcher LM.
Limit the assessment to no more than two hours.
Provide reimbursement for reasonable travel expenses.

steps.title: Conduct research assessment
steps.instruction: Perform a standardized interview, brief cognitive tests, brief neurological examination, and a battery of questionnaires, recording all behavioural and linguistic features.

substeps.instruction: Administer the following measures:
• Green’s Medical Symptom Validity Test (licensed; £620 for 100 uses, funded from CCBS discretionary fund).
• Coin‑in‑hand test (10 trials, participant must remember which hand holds a coin).
• Subjective Memory Complaint 5‑point Likert scale (“In general, how would you rate your memory?”).
• Record presence of a spouse/partner/sibling/parent with dementia (Y/N) and relationship description.
• Record daily contact or caring for a person with dementia (Y/N).
• Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (English version 7.0.2 for DSM‑5).
• PHQ‑15 physical symptoms questionnaire (including extra questions used in the Scottish Neurological Symptoms Study).
• Binary outcome (FCD / not FCD) based on the researcher’s opinion at the end of the assessment.
Observe and record behavioural markers:
– Length of first turn (head turns, few words, answer > a few seconds).
– Responses to prompts such as “Tell me about a time your memory failed you.” (head turn, vague vs detailed example, timescale).
– Presence of a second example or “don’t know” response.
– Ability to answer compound questions (0/2, 1/2, or both parts).
– Repetitions (with or without marking).
– Report of premorbid memory (normal/poor vs “brilliant”).
– Immediate vs delayed recall ratio (delayed < immediate or vice‑versa).
– Time each response with a stopwatch (from end of instruction to end of response; note consistency).
– Gait and coordination (primarily to observe ability to follow instructions).
All responses are timed and noted.

steps.title: Obtain written informed consent
steps.instruction: On the day of the research assessment, obtain written informed consent before any protocol‑specific procedures are performed.

substeps.instruction: Confirm that the participant has previously received and read the PIS, has had the study explained, and has had all questions answered.
Sign and date the Informed Consent Form in the presence of the participant; give the participant a copy and file one copy in the Investigator Site File and the participant’s medical notes.

steps.title: Store data securely
steps.instruction: Enter all collected data into password‑protected electronic systems and store paper records in locked cabinets.

substeps.instruction: Electronic data: NHS Lothian servers and University of Edinburgh servers, accessible only to Dr Laura McWhirter.
Paper CRFs: pseudonymised by study number, stored in locked filing cabinet at the Kennedy Tower, University of Edinburgh; key stored within the Kennedy Tower and accessible to Dr McWhirter.
Participant contact details (name, DOB, address, phone, email) stored in a separate locked cabinet, also at the Kennedy Tower.
Retain personal data for five years after participation; retain all study documentation for a minimum of three years after study end.

steps.title: Panel reference diagnosis (Panel Diagnosis A)
steps.instruction: Establish the reference standard diagnosis for each participant via a consensus panel.

substeps.instruction: Panel composition: Consultant Neurologist, Consultant Neuropsychiatrist, Consultant Psychiatrist of Ageing.
Panel chair: the researcher who performed the research assessments (LM).
Provide the panel with the participant’s clinical history, past medical history, clinical notes, clinic letter, electronic medical record, neuroimaging reports, and any other investigations.
Panel records the consensus diagnosis (Panel Diagnosis A) on the case report form (CRF) in ink before receiving any further staged information.

steps.title: Staged additional panel diagnoses
steps.instruction: Present additional information to the panel in stages and record diagnoses at each stage.

substeps.instruction: After Panel Diagnosis A is finalised, supply further data (e.g., advanced imaging, CSF AD biomarker profile) and ask the panel to re‑evaluate, producing Panel Diagnoses B and C1‑C5.
Record each staged diagnosis on the CRF.
Document the likelihood that each new piece of information would influence the diagnosis for later use in the scoring‑tool development.

steps.title: Follow‑up electronic‑record review
steps.instruction: One to two years after the initial clinical assessment, review participants’ electronic medical records for outcome changes.

substeps.instruction: A blinded researcher checks for (a) resolution of cognitive symptoms, (b) change of diagnosis to dementia, or (c) death.
If the EMR is unclear, telephone the participant’s GP practice to obtain clarification.

steps.title: Data analysis and scoring‑tool development
steps.instruction: Analyze collected data to identify the most predictive assessment elements and create a diagnostic scoring tool.

substeps.instruction: Perform factor analysis to determine which interview, cognitive, neurological, and questionnaire items best predict Panel Diagnosis A, adjusting for demographics and pre‑test probability.
Conduct secondary analysis to assess whether information from the research assessment changes panel opinion (compare Panel Diagnosis B to A).
Combine the elements with greatest utility into a diagnostic scoring tool for functional cognitive disorder.

steps.title: Sample‑size justification
steps.instruction: Recruit a minimum of 115 participants based on prevalence and accuracy assumptions.

substeps.instruction: Assume functional cognitive disorder prevalence of 30 % in the study population.
Assume test sensitivity of 90 % and specificity of 90 %.
Calculate that at least 115 participants are required to achieve the desired precision.

steps.title: Ethical and regulatory compliance
steps.instruction: Secure approvals, register the protocol, and maintain GCP and data‑protection standards throughout the study.

substeps.instruction: Obtain ethical approval from the South East Scotland Research Ethics Committee (December 2018 – February 2019).
Pre‑register the protocol at protocols.io; plan to share anonymised data via the Edinburgh Datashare repository.
Ensure all investigators are familiar with the protocol; delegate tasks on a Delegation Log signed by all staff before they perform study procedures.
Record any protocol deviations in a deviation log and report serious breaches within 24 hours to the co‑sponsors (seriousbreach@accord.scot).
Submit amendments to the sponsor and REC before enrolling participants under the amended protocol.
Maintain study documentation for at least three years after the defined end of study (last participant’s last visit).
Report study closure to the REC, R&D offices, and co‑sponsors within 90 days (or 15 days if terminated early).

steps.title: Study timeline
steps.instruction: Follow the predefined chronological milestones for the project.

substeps.instruction: December 2018 – February 2019: Apply for and obtain ethical approval.
March 2019 – May 2020: Recruit participants and collect baseline data.
June 2020 – December 2021: Conduct follow‑up, perform data analysis, and write up results.
